recommended_metric.reasoning: target is imbalanced (0.32) and goal is 'predict readmission risk' — missing a true readmission (false negative) is likely more costly than a false alarm, so recall should be prioritized over raw accuracy or precision. F1 tracked secondarily to keep an eye on precision, since optimizing recall alone risks too many false alarms. ROC-AUC included as a threshold-independent secondary check; at 0.32 positive rate the imbalance isn't severe enough to prefer PR-AUC over ROC-AUC the way it would be under a more extreme skew (e.g. <5% positive).

recommended_strategy.narrative: Wide dataset with several high-cardinality categorical fields — tree-based models and target/frequency encoding likely outperform one-hot + linear models. Normalize gender categories and drop PII/leakage columns before preprocessing. Start with blood_sugar given strongest target correlation. Given 87 candidate columns, an incremental (wrapper-style, forward-selection) posture is recommended over starting broad — one-at-a-time addition, evidence-driven by Diagnosis each iteration, is worth its cost at this width; a small dataset would favor starting with more features and pruning instead. Tree-based models chosen above will also apply embedded feature importance automatically during Training, complementing this incremental process rather than replacing it.

plots.reason: blood_sugar is the highest-correlating numeric feature (Spearman 0.41) — a histogram answers the specific question of whether its distribution is well-behaved enough for direct use or needs transformation before modeling. A scatter against the target would show the feature-target relationship, but not the marginal shape; the histogram is the right first check because skew and outliers here would affect both imputation strategy (median vs. mean) and whether a log transform is warranted before encoding the relationship.
plots.insight: The distribution is right-skewed with a long tail extending past 250 mg/dL, while the bulk of values cluster between 80–180 — a ~3:1 ratio between the IQR core and the tail. This shape is consistent with the 12 outliers already flagged by the IQR check. In clinical terms, values above ~200 represent overt hyperglycemia, a known readmission risk factor, so the tail is likely real signal rather than data entry error — clipping it would discard the exact cases where the feature is most predictive. The right skew means a log or square-root transform is worth trying before using this feature in distance-based or linear models; tree-based models are less sensitive to this. For imputation (2% missing, MCAR): median is the correct choice over mean given the skew — mean would be pulled up by the tail and would overestimate a typical missing value.

plots.reason: a class balance bar chart is mandatory for any classification task because it determines whether accuracy is a misleading metric and whether the model needs class-weight adjustment or resampling. A histogram of the target would show the same information but a bar chart is clearer for a two-class discrete outcome and is the standard reference a reviewer expects to see alongside the metric recommendation.
plots.insight: The positive class (readmission) makes up 32% of rows, leaving 68% as negative — a moderate imbalance, not a severe one. At this ratio, a model that always predicts negative would score 68% accuracy, making accuracy a misleading headline metric; this directly drives the recall-primary recommendation in `recommended_metric`. The imbalance is not severe enough (it would need to be below roughly 10% positive) to justify resampling techniques like SMOTE or undersampling, which introduce their own distortions. Instead, using class weights during training (setting the positive class weight to ~2.1×) is the right first adjustment — this is a flag for Training, not Preprocess. The region=east segment's 0.52 positive rate (vs. 0.32 overall) means the class balance looks meaningfully different by region; if the model is deployed nationally, per-region calibration may matter.
